column1: Roughly how many requests per second is 1 million requests per day?
column2: About 12 per second. Divide daily volume by ~10^5 (86,400 seconds per day), then multiply by 2-3 for the peak.

column1: What does the CAP theorem actually force you to choose?
column2: During a network partition, a system must give up either consistency (linearizability) or availability. Partition tolerance is not optional, so “pick 2 of 3” is a misstatement.

column1: What does PACELC add to CAP?
column2: The normal case: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Most of the time the real trade-off is latency vs consistency.

column1: List the 9 steps of the design framework.
column2: Clarify requirements, estimate capacity, define the API, design the data model, sketch the high-level design, deep dive, discuss trade-offs, address bottlenecks, handle follow-ups.

column1: What separates a staff-level design answer from a senior one?
column2: Staff answers question the requirements, find the one or two things that decide the design, choose deep dives by risk, and tie trade-offs to business and operational cost.

column1: Which anomaly does snapshot isolation still allow?
column2: Write skew: two transactions read the same data and each writes a different row, together breaking a rule neither broke alone.

column1: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and what does it let through?
column2: Read Committed. Each statement sees a fresh snapshot, so read-then-write logic can suffer lost updates and write skew.

column1: Name three fixes for a lost update.
column2: An atomic UPDATE (SET n = n + 1), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before writing, or an optimistic version column checked in the WHERE clause.

column1: B-tree vs LSM-tree: which favours writes, and why?
column2: LSM-tree. It appends to an in-memory memtable and flushes sorted immutable files that are merged later; a B-tree updates pages in place.

column1: What can a Bloom filter answer with certainty?
column2: “Definitely not present.” “Present” may be a false positive. About 10 bits per key gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate.

column1: Why do column stores beat row stores for analytics?
column2: A query reads only the columns it needs, similar values stored together compress far better (dictionary, run-length), and min/max statistics let it skip blocks.

column1: When data changes, should you update or delete the cached copy?
column2: Delete it. Two racing writers that overwrite the cache can leave stale data cached indefinitely.

column1: Why doesn't sharding fix a hot key?
column2: All the traffic is on one key, so it lands on one shard however many shards exist. Use an in-process L1 cache, replicate the key, or serve it from the CDN.

column1: Cache penetration vs cache avalanche?
column2: Penetration: requests for keys that exist nowhere bypass the cache every time (cache negative results or use a Bloom filter). Avalanche: many keys expire at once (add jitter to TTLs).

column1: What data should never be cached?
column2: Data that must be exactly right at read time, such as bank balances or inventory counts used to make decisions.

column1: What are a token bucket's two parameters, and what behaviour do they allow?
column2: Capacity (burst size) and refill rate. Short bursts up to capacity are allowed while the long-run rate is enforced.

column1: L4 vs L7 load balancing?
column2: L4 routes by IP and port without reading the request; L7 reads HTTP (paths, headers, cookies) and can route by content, at more CPU cost.

column1: Why must INCR and EXPIRE for a rate limiter be atomic?
column2: A crash between two separate calls leaves a counter with no TTL, which becomes a permanent ban. Pipeline them or use a Lua script.

column1: What is the Kubernetes HPA scaling rule?
column2: desired = ceil(current x metric / target), skipped within a +-10% tolerance. Scale-down uses the highest recommendation of the last 5 minutes; scale-up is immediate.

column1: Why isn't autoscaling overload protection?
column2: New capacity takes minutes to detect, boot and warm up. Spikes faster than that hit existing capacity, so you also need headroom and load shedding.

column1: Is exactly-once delivery possible over a network?
column2: No. You get at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, or exactly-once processing inside one system's transaction boundary (e.g. Kafka transactions).

column1: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
column2: The dual write: a database update and an event publish can't share a transaction. Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it afterwards (or use CDC).

column1: Kafka guarantees ordering within what unit?
column2: A partition. Messages that must stay in order need the same key, so they land on the same partition.

column1: What is a watermark in stream processing?
column2: The processor's assertion that no more events older than time W are expected. Windows that end before W are emitted; later arrivals are late data.

column1: How do you make a stream job's output exactly-once in effect?
column2: Upsert each window's final value keyed by (key, window) instead of incrementing, so a replay overwrites rather than double-counts.

column1: Backward vs forward schema compatibility?
column2: Backward: new readers can read old data (add fields with defaults; upgrade consumers first). Forward: old readers can read new data (upgrade producers first).

column1: What is a saga?
column2: A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. It replaces a distributed transaction across services.

column1: How do you rename a database column with zero downtime?
column2: Expand/contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old column, then drop it later. Each step is deployable and reversible alone.

column1: Why can a metadata-only ALTER TABLE take a PostgreSQL site down?
column2: It queues for an exclusive lock behind a long-running query, and every new query on the table queues behind it. Set lock_timeout and retry.

column1: What should a canary be compared against?
column2: A fresh baseline of the current version, started at the same time and size, not the old fleet, which differs in uptime and warm caches.

column1: What is the difference between deploy and release?
column2: Deploy puts code on servers; release exposes behaviour to users. Feature flags separate the two, so a release can be rolled out gradually or turned off in seconds.

column1: Why add jitter to retries?
column2: Clients that failed together otherwise retry together in synchronized waves. Full jitter waits a random time between 0 and the backoff cap.

column1: What does a circuit breaker do?
column2: After repeated failures it opens and fails fast without calling the dependency, then lets a trial request through (half-open) to test recovery.

column1: State Little's Law.
column2: Requests in flight = throughput x latency. For example, 1,000 req/s at 200 ms means 200 concurrent requests.

column1: How much downtime does a 99.9% monthly SLO allow?
column2: About 43 minutes per month: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes.

column1: Backpressure vs load shedding?
column2: Backpressure rejects work early when a bounded queue is full, so callers slow down. Load shedding deliberately drops the least valuable work first when demand exceeds capacity.

column1: How many failures can a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate?
column2: Two. A majority (3) is needed. Even sizes add nothing: 4 nodes tolerate 1 failure, the same as 3.

column1: What is a fencing token, and who issues it?
column2: A monotonically increasing number issued by the lock service with each grant. Storage rejects writes carrying a lower token than the highest it has seen.

column1: Lamport clocks vs vector clocks?
column2: Lamport timestamps give an order consistent with causality but can't detect concurrency. Vector clocks can tell “happened before” from “concurrent”.

column1: What does a phi accrual failure detector output?
column2: A suspicion level, phi = -log10(probability a heartbeat would arrive even later), that adapts to observed jitter instead of using a fixed timeout.

column1: How fast does gossip spread news through N nodes?
column2: In about O(log N) rounds, roughly log2 N + ln N with fanout 1: around 17 rounds for 1,000 nodes.

column1: Does W + R > N give linearizable reads?
column2: No. It guarantees that read and write quorums overlap, but sloppy quorums, partially failed writes and concurrent updates still allow stale or conflicting reads.

column1: Why use Merkle trees for anti-entropy?
column2: Replicas compare root hashes and descend only into subtrees that differ, finding a few stale keys among millions with tens of hash comparisons.

column1: How many codes do 7 base62 characters give?
column2: 62^7, about 3.5 trillion.

column1: Why not expose a sequential counter directly as the short code?
column2: Sequential codes are trivial to enumerate. Run the counter through a secret bijection before making it public.

column1: Why is caching a URL shortener nearly free?
column2: Mappings are immutable, so there is no invalidation problem; an in-process cache and long CDN TTLs absorb most reads.

column1: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read?
column2: Write: push each post into followers' feeds when posted (fast reads, explodes for celebrities). Read: assemble the feed at read time (cheap writes, slow reads). Production systems use a hybrid.

column1: What ordering should a chat system guarantee?
column2: Order within a conversation, assigned server-side with sequence numbers. Global ordering is unnecessary, and client clocks can't be trusted.

column1: How does a chat server deliver a message to a user connected elsewhere?
column2: Through a connection registry that maps each user to the server holding their WebSocket; no server can reach a user it doesn't know about.

column1: Why does a sync client split files into chunks?
column2: Only changed chunks are uploaded (delta sync), uploads resume chunk by chunk, and identical chunks deduplicate by content hash.

column1: What is adaptive bitrate streaming?
column2: Video is encoded at several bitrates and cut into short segments; the player picks each segment's quality from measured bandwidth (HLS, DASH).

column1: Why upload large files with presigned URLs?
column2: The client uploads straight to object storage, so application servers never hold the bytes; the URL grants one operation on one key until it expires.

column1: RS(10,4) erasure coding vs 3x replication?
column2: 1.4x vs 3x storage. RS(10,4) survives any 4 lost fragments vs 2 lost copies, but repairing one fragment reads 10 others.

column1: Who should mint the idempotency key for a payment, client or server?
column2: The client. A key the server generates on each retry defeats the mechanism.

column1: Why claim the idempotency key with SET NX before charging?
column2: Check-then-set lets two concurrent retries both pass the check and double-charge. An atomic claim lets only one through.

column1: How should money be stored?
column2: As integer minor units (cents), never floats, and totals recomputed server-side from authoritative prices.

column1: Why is reconciliation required in a payment system?
column2: It is the only backstop for a charge that succeeded at the gateway but never reached your ledger (or the reverse).

column1: Authentication vs authorization?
column2: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what that identity may do.

column1: How should passwords be stored?
column2: With a slow, salted, memory-hard hash such as Argon2id. Never encrypted, and never with a fast hash like SHA-256.

column1: What is envelope encryption?
column2: Data is encrypted with a data key (DEK), and the DEK is encrypted by a key held in a KMS, so keys can be rotated and access audited without re-encrypting everything.

column1: REST, gRPC or GraphQL: what should decide?
column2: The consumer: REST for broad public APIs, gRPC for internal service-to-service calls, GraphQL for clients that need flexible, aggregated reads.

column1: Why prefer cursor pagination over offset pagination?
column2: Offsets get slower as they grow and skip or repeat items when data changes; a cursor continues from a stable position.

column1: What makes an API change breaking?
column2: Removing or renaming a field, tightening validation, changing a type, or changing a field's meaning. Adding an optional field or endpoint is safe.

column1: Why can't you average percentiles?
column2: The p99 of several hosts is not the average of their p99s. Aggregate histogram buckets (distributions), then compute the percentile.

column1: What drives the cost of a metrics system?
column2: Cardinality: the product of label values. Unbounded dimensions such as user IDs belong in traces and logs.

column1: Metrics, traces, logs: what does each do best?
column2: Metrics detect, traces localize, logs explain, in that order.

column1: Mitigate or diagnose first during an incident?
column2: Mitigate. A rollback or a flag flip ends user harm far faster than understanding the cause.

column1: What should a page be triggered by?
column2: User-facing symptoms and error-budget burn rates, not causes or fixed thresholds such as CPU > 80%.

column1: What does the Incident Commander do?
column2: Coordinates and decides, but fixes nothing; one other person makes changes to production, announcing each one.

column1: What is training/serving skew?
column2: Features computed differently in training and in serving drift apart. Use one feature definition, or log the exact features served and train on them.

column1: How must features be joined for training data?
column2: As of the prediction time (point-in-time correct), never as of query time, or future information leaks into training.

column1: Why does retrieval optimize recall in a ranking funnel?
column2: Nothing downstream can recover a candidate that retrieval dropped; later stages trade recall for precision.

column1: What usually limits LLM serving throughput: compute or memory?
column2: Memory, specifically the KV cache, which grows with batch size and sequence length.

column1: How do you size the KV cache per token?
column2: 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes per value.

column1: What does PagedAttention change?
column2: It stores the KV cache in fixed-size pages allocated on demand, like OS virtual memory, instead of contiguous pre-allocated blocks.

column1: Why is continuous batching standard?
column2: Static batching waits for the slowest sequence while finished slots idle; continuous batching swaps in new requests every step.

column1: Why rerank retrieved results?
column2: A cross-encoder reranker over the top candidates is the cheapest, highest-leverage retrieval quality improvement.

column1: Why does reciprocal rank fusion beat weighted score fusion?
column2: It combines ranks, which are comparable across retrievers, instead of raw scores, which are not.

column1: Does a bigger context window remove the need for retrieval?
column2: No. Cost, latency and lost-in-the-middle effects remain; more context is not more accuracy.

column1: What is the main design surface of an agent?
column2: The harness: tools, middleware and context management, more than the choice of model.

column1: How should agent tools be designed?
column2: Fewer, larger, orthogonal tools at the level of the agent's intent, with errors that say what to do next.

column1: Why treat the context window as a budget?
column2: Quality degrades long before the hard limit, so context must be written, selected, compressed and isolated deliberately.

column1: Why report Cohen's kappa instead of raw agreement for an LLM judge?
column2: Raw agreement is inflated by the base rate; kappa measures agreement beyond chance.

column1: Binary rubric questions or 1-5 scales?
column2: Binary questions: they are more reliable and easier to validate against human labels.

column1: Why must eval results carry a confidence interval?
column2: Small samples hide large differences: at n=50 an 80% pass rate has a 95% interval about +-11 points.

column1: Why route queries by complexity?
column2: Sending every query to the largest model overspends severalfold; simple queries can go to cheaper models.

column1: How should retrieved documents and tool results be treated?
column2: As untrusted data, never as instructions, because they are a prompt-injection vector.

column1: Why must guardrails cover both input and output?
column2: An input filter alone still lets PII and unsafe content out through the model's responses.

column1: How does a trie serve autocomplete fast?
column2: Each node caches the top-k completions for its prefix, so a keystroke is one lookup instead of a subtree walk.

column1: Why search 9 geohash cells for “nearby”?
column2: Near points can sit in adjacent cells with no shared prefix; search the cell and its 8 neighbours, then filter by exact distance.

column1: Why partition a search index by document rather than by term?
column2: Each shard answers multi-term queries locally and returns a small top-k; term partitioning ships large posting lists between shards.

column1: How do you stop a seat being sold twice?
column2: A conditional update: UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'available' (or the hold expired), then check that the number of rows updated is what you asked for.

column1: Why does a hold expiry need no background job for correctness?
column2: Expired holds are treated as free in the next buyer's WHERE clause; a sweeper only tidies the seat map.

column1: What does a virtual waiting room change?
column2: The booking tier's load becomes a chosen admission rate instead of the size of the crowd; signed tokens enforce it at the gateway.

column1: How do you handle payment racing an expiring hold?
column2: Authorize the card, confirm the seat conditionally on the hold, then capture, or void the authorization if the hold expired.

column1: What limits a polite crawler's throughput?
column2: The number of distinct hosts with URLs ready, because each host gets about one request per second, not the number of machines.

column1: Why partition a crawl by host hash rather than URL hash?
column2: Each host's queue and rate timer then live on one worker, so politeness needs no coordination.

column1: What is SimHash used for?
column2: Near-duplicate detection: similar pages get 64-bit fingerprints that differ in a few bits (Google used a 3-bit threshold).

column1: Why give transactional notifications their own queues?
column2: So a marketing blast can never delay a one-time passcode or a password reset.

column1: What does acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 guarantee in Kafka?
column2: An acknowledged write is on every in-sync replica, and on at least 2, so a leader failure can't lose it; with fewer in-sync replicas, writes are refused.

column1: What is the high watermark?
column2: The highest offset present on every in-sync replica; consumers only see messages below it.

column1: Why does Gorilla compression work so well on metrics?
column2: Regular scrape intervals make delta-of-delta timestamps usually zero (1 bit), and slowly changing values XOR to few differing bits.

column1: What should downsampling keep per interval?
column2: Sum, count, min and max (and histogram buckets), so averages and percentiles can still be computed correctly.
